Maladaptive Strategies.value: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
I try hard to control my emotions

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't rely on other people
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Partial Clarity' implies marked fragmentation with important gaps, while 'Vivid Memory' implies globally clear and detailed recall. These can sometimes coexist for specific segments, but stated together at face value they pull in opposite directions and are the clearest internal inconsistency in the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: The profile lacks any Threat items, despite terrorism-related avoidance of crowds and enclosed/public spaces usually being linked to a current sense of danger in public places. With Triggers→Threat inactive and no Threat node content provided, the avoidance pattern is left clinically unanchored.

issues.item: Avoid Crowds: Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events
issues.explanation: Memory items describe vivid, cue-driven, sensory re-experiencing, especially being triggered by surroundings without warning. However, all Triggers edges are inactive and no Trigger items are present, making the specific 'surroundings instantly bring back the full memory' item poorly aligned with the formulation structure.

issues.item: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
issues.explanation: Negative appraisals focus on generalized mistrust of self, body, and others, while the maladaptive strategies are highly situational (crowds/enclosed spaces). Without corresponding threat or trigger content, these nodes do not form a clearly coherent terrorism-specific presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: The Memory item describes strong cue-driven reactivation by surroundings, but the formulation explicitly has Triggers inactive with Memory. This creates a direct contradiction between the item's content and the formulation structure.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Crowds: Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events
issues.explanation: Avoiding crowds is plausible after terrorism, but it implies salient environmental trigger sensitivity and public-place threat anticipation. In this profile, Triggers and Threat are not represented and are inactive in the formulation, so this strategy lacks a coherent linked context.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: Checking surroundings for signs of threat implies an active trigger/threat monitoring pattern, but the formulation explicitly has Triggers and Threat disconnected from the rest of the system, making this item poorly aligned with the cognitive formulation.

issues.item: Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
issues.explanation: Frequent reassurance seeking from others sits awkwardly with the simultaneous appraisal 'I can't rely on other people.' While some ambivalence is possible, taking both as central items without any moderating context creates a notable cross-node tension.

issues.item: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'I can no longer trust my own body' is more typical of trauma involving physical injury, illness, or prominent somatic threat. With terrorism trauma, it is not impossible, but alongside the other selected items there is little memory content or appraisal content explaining bodily unreliability, so this item feels weakly grounded in the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Koa was a 71-year-old single painter of Pacific Islander background who had spent most of his adult life working with his hands, moving between rooms and job sites with the steady routine of a man who preferred practical tasks to fuss. Before the attack, he described himself as private but capable, someone who got on with people without needing much from them. That changed the evening a terrorist bombing tore through a crowded public place where he had been passing through. He remembered the noise first, then the sudden violence of bodies hitting the ground and the confusion of not knowing where the danger was coming from. In the middle of it, he had been forced down into a position that his body still seemed to remember with awful precision, and he later said that when the memory returned, it was not like watching a scene from outside but like being thrown back into that same cramped posture, his muscles braced as if he were still pinned there.

In the weeks afterward, Koa found that the event would force its way into his mind without warning. A sound, a crowded pavement, or even a moment of idleness could bring it back with no invitation, and when it did, the details were strikingly clear to him. He could see and hear the scene with a vividness that unsettled him, as though the memory had been preserved in exact detail and refused to fade. What distressed him most was that the recollection did not stay contained in thought; it took on a bodily quality, so that he would feel his torso tense and his limbs lock in the same position he associated with the attack. He would sit very still when this happened, waiting for the sensation to pass, trying not to let anyone notice how much it affected him.

As time went on, Koa became increasingly convinced that he could not trust himself to keep steady. He was a man who had once prided himself on being self-reliant, but after the bombing he began to doubt his own judgment and composure. If he felt a wave of panic building, he would worry that he would not manage it well, or that he might not cope if he had to face another unexpected event alone. At the same time, he found it hard to trust other people. The attack had occurred among strangers in an ordinary public setting, and afterward he came to believe that the world could turn dangerous without warning and that other people might not be dependable when it mattered. He did not talk about this dramatically; rather, it sat behind his decisions, making him more cautious and less willing to place himself in situations where he would have to depend on anyone else.

By the time he sought help, these beliefs had settled into daily habits. Koa had started asking people around him for reassurance that he was okay, checking in more than he used to, almost needing others to confirm that he was safe, stable, and not about to fall apart. He was aware that he leaned on these conversations, but they gave him temporary relief when the fear felt close. He also tried hard to control his emotions, keeping his voice measured and his face composed even when the memory had been stirred up. He spoke about this with some shame, saying he did not want to become "a burden" or look weak in front of others. The effort took energy, and at times he felt exhausted by holding himself in check, but he remained committed to appearing controlled.

Avoiding going out gradually became another part of his life. As a painter, Koa had long been used to moving between houses, shops, and building sites, but after the bombing he began turning down some work and limiting where he would go. The ordinary demands of his occupation meant that he could not stay inside all the time, yet even routine trips could leave him on edge if the setting felt crowded or unpredictable. He became more selective about when he would leave home, often arranging his day around the hope of not encountering anything too busy or exposed. This narrowing of his world carried practical consequences: his work became less regular, and his days grew smaller, organized around what felt manageable rather than what he might once have done without thought.

By the present, Koa had reached a point where he was tired of living with the memory arriving on its own, tired of needing repeated reassurance, and tired of feeling that the outside world remained unsafe. He came to treatment not because he believed the fear was irrational, but because he no longer wanted his life to be shaped so tightly around it. What he wanted most was to feel that he could go out again without bracing for disaster, and what frightened him most was the possibility that he would remain stuck believing neither himself nor other people could be relied on when it mattered.
